articles.title: Less than 4 years from development goals deadline, progress shows what’s possible
articles.summary: For Benin, making progress on the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) has meant finding new ways to finance development.
articles.content:
The West African country has increased domestic revenue by 0.5 per cent of GDP each year for the past decade, issued Africa’s first SDG bond in 2021 and used the resulting funding to expand access to education and drinking water, Aristide Medenou, Benin’s minister of economic cooperation, said on Friday.

Access to drinking water there has increased from 40 per cent to 80 per cent in the past five years, Mr. Medenou said, while a new industrial zone launched in 2021 has created 25,000 jobs.

“If a country is not able to increase the domestic revenue, the country cannot go forward in implementing the SDGs,” Mr. Medenou said at the UN’s annual SDG Moment event ahead of the General Assembly’s High-Level Week in New York.

Even as the world remains far from achieving the SDGs, Mr. Medenou said Benin offers a concrete example of governments translating commitments into beneficial policies.

Many goals off track

In 2015, all UN Member States adopted the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, committing to 17 SDGs focusing on issues such as ending poverty, protecting the planet and ensuring lasting peace.

Member States set a target to achieve these goals by 2030. However, the UN’s most recent progress report indicated that progress on the goals is slow and uneven – of the 139 targets with available trend data, 36 per cent are on track or making moderate progress.

“Progress was never automatic,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres said on Friday. “It was earned through the determination of people, communities and countries.”

SDGs create meaningful progress

At UN Headquarters in New York, UN officials and world leaders highlighted both the gains made over the past decade – and the scale of the remaining challenge.

Nearly a billion people have gained access to safely managed drinking water since the SDGs were adopted, and 1.2 billion have gained access to safely managed sanitation. Electricity now reaches 92 per cent of the world’s population – up from 87 per cent in 2015 – and internet access has risen from 40 per cent to 74 per cent.

But 49 per cent of SDG targets with available trend data are progressing too slowly, while 15 per cent have fallen below their 2015 baselines, according to the SDG Progress Report.

Food insecurity affected 2.1 billion people in 2025, while one in 10 people still live in extreme poverty, said General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman.

The world faces a $4 trillion annual SDG financing gap, while official development assistance fell by a record 23 per cent in 2025. In many countries, debt payments outstrip spending on social services.

The world is currently on track to warm by around 2.8 degrees Celsius this century, well above the 1.5-degree threshold set by the Paris Agreement.

“These are losses that many cannot absorb,” Mr. Rahman said. “For many of us, sustainability is a matter of life and death.”

UN Photo/Manuel Elías

Young leaders call for action

Suzuka Nakamura of Japan and Adelin Pierre of Haiti, two of the UN’s Young Leaders for the SDGs, called on governments to act with the same urgency that led them to agree on the SDGs 11 years ago.

“To the leaders in this room and around the world, you made this promise,” Ms. Nakamura said. “We are asking you to keep it.”

Mr. Medenou also stressed the need to involve the private sector, saying governments “cannot do it alone.”

‘Powerful headwinds’ to SDG progress

Mr. Guterres said the lives that have been improved by SDG implementation demonstrate that multilateral cooperation can produce tangible improvements when governments act.

He explained that the pursuit of the goals has helped reduce child and maternal mortality, prevent millions of new HIV infections, and expand access to education, social protection, renewable energy and other services.

But progress faces “powerful headwinds” such as conflicts, weakened international cooperation, the climate crisis, attacks on the rights of women and girls, and debt and investment constraints, Mr. Guterres said.

“The promises governments made in adopting the Goals are not being kept,” he said. “It is time to keep them.”

Peace a prerequisite

Tweet URL

The Secretary-General emphasised the priorities of fighting inequality, protecting the planet, financing sustainable development and using all available tools and technologies to accelerate progress.

He called for greater investment in education and health, a just transition to renewable energy, stronger financing and debt support for developing countries, and greater use of technology such as “responsible” artificial intelligence.

Mr. Guterres said peace is both a foundation and an enabler of sustainable development, stressing that the world needs renewed efforts to secure peace everywhere.

There’s still time

With four years until the deadline, speakers emphasised the need to convert commitments into results while reaching the people who remain the furthest behind.

UN Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) President Amar Bendjama said progress is possible when ambition is matched with implementation.

For the young leaders at the event, the impending deadline is not a reason to abandon the goals, but a reason to act with increased urgency.

“There is still time to act, but we need to move together,” Ms. Nakamura said. “We are not giving up hope on the SDGs, and neither should you.”

articles.personality_title: Benin’s smart funding boosts water, jobs and education as UN urges faster SDG progress
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In 2015, countries around the world agreed on 17 goals called the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) to fight poverty, protect the planet, and improve lives by 2030. But progress has been slow and uneven, with many targets still far from being met.

**What happened** – Benin, a country in West Africa, has found new ways to pay for its development. Over the past decade, it raised more money within the country each year and in 2021 issued Africa’s first SDG bond, a special loan that funds projects linked to the SDGs. Using this money, Benin doubled the number of people with clean drinking water from 40% to 80% in five years and created 25,000 jobs in a new industrial zone.

**Impact** – Benin’s example shows how smart financing and government action can turn promises into real improvements. While many countries struggle with funding and challenges like climate change and conflict, Benin’s progress on water, jobs, and education provides a clear example of what is possible when resources are used well.

**What's next step** – The United Nations and world leaders say there is still time to meet the SDGs by 2030, but countries need to act faster. This includes investing more in education and health, using new technologies responsibly, supporting developing countries with debt relief, and promoting peace, which is essential for lasting development.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Benin’s success in funding and delivering basic services highlights how focused action can advance global development goals even as the world races against time.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le financement innovant du Bénin améliore l’eau, l’emploi et l’éducation alors que l’ONU appelle à accélérer les progrès des ODD
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En 2015, les pays du monde entier ont adopté 17 objectifs appelés Objectifs de Développement Durable (ODD) pour lutter contre la pauvreté, protéger la planète et améliorer la vie d’ici 2030. Mais les progrès ont été lents et inégaux, avec de nombreux objectifs encore loin d’être atteints.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le Bénin, un pays d’Afrique de l’Ouest, a trouvé de nouvelles façons de financer son développement. Au cours de la dernière décennie, il a augmenté chaque année ses recettes intérieures et, en 2021, a émis la première obligation liée aux ODD en Afrique. Grâce à ces fonds, le Bénin a doublé le nombre de personnes ayant accès à l’eau potable, passant de 40 % à 80 % en cinq ans, et a créé 25 000 emplois dans une nouvelle zone industrielle.

**Impact** – L’exemple du Bénin montre comment un financement intelligent et une action gouvernementale peuvent transformer les promesses en améliorations concrètes. Alors que de nombreux pays font face à des défis comme le changement climatique ou les conflits, les progrès du Bénin en matière d’eau, d’emplois et d’éducation illustrent ce qui est possible quand les ressources sont bien utilisées.

**Prochaine étape** – L’ONU et les dirigeants mondiaux affirment qu’il reste encore du temps pour atteindre les ODD d’ici 2030, mais les pays doivent agir plus rapidement. Cela inclut plus d’investissements dans l’éducation et la santé, l’utilisation responsable de nouvelles technologies, le soutien aux pays en développement avec l’allègement de la dette, et la promotion de la paix, essentielle pour un développement durable.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Le succès du Bénin dans le financement et la fourniture de services de base montre que des actions ciblées peuvent faire avancer les objectifs mondiaux de développement même face à l’urgence du temps.
articles.personality_title_es: El financiamiento inteligente de Benín mejora agua, empleos y educación mientras la ONU pide acelerar el progreso de los ODS
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En 2015, países de todo el mundo acordaron 17 objetivos llamados Objetivos de Desarrollo Sostenible (ODS) para acabar con la pobreza, proteger el planeta y mejorar la vida para 2030. Pero los avances han sido lentos y desiguales, y muchas metas aún están lejos de cumplirse.

**Qué pasó** – Benín, un país de África Occidental, encontró nuevas formas de financiar su desarrollo. Durante la última década, aumentó cada año sus ingresos internos y en 2021 emitió el primer bono ligado a los ODS en África. Con estos fondos, Benín duplicó el acceso al agua potable del 40 % al 80 % en cinco años y creó 25,000 empleos en una nueva zona industrial.

**Impacto** – El ejemplo de Benín muestra cómo una financiación inteligente y la acción del gobierno pueden convertir promesas en mejoras concretas. Mientras muchos países enfrentan desafíos como el cambio climático y conflictos, los avances de Benín en agua, empleos y educación demuestran lo que es posible cuando se usan bien los recursos.

**Próximo paso** – La ONU y líderes mundiales dicen que aún hay tiempo para alcanzar los ODS para 2030, pero los países deben actuar más rápido. Esto incluye invertir más en educación y salud, usar nuevas tecnologías con responsabilidad, apoyar a los países en desarrollo con alivio de deuda y promover la paz, que es esencial para el desarrollo duradero.

**Resumen en una frase** – El éxito de Benín en financiar y entregar servicios básicos muestra cómo acciones enfocadas pueden avanzar los objetivos globales de desarrollo a pesar de la urgencia del tiempo.
